"Inform on" is a phrasal verb. It means to secretly tell an authority figure about something wrong, illegal, or against the rules that another person has done.

When you "inform on" someone, you are going to a person in power — like the police, a teacher, a boss, or a government official — and giving them information that gets the other person into trouble.

Think of it this way:

Person A does something wrong. Person B finds out. Person B goes to an authority and tells them what Person A did. Person B has informed on Person A.
Breaking It Down — Word by Word

• "Inform" on its own just means to tell or to give information. It is a perfectly neutral word.
  • "On" is what makes this phrase special. When you add "on," the word shifts. You are no longer just telling someone something — you are telling against someone. The "on" points the information like an arrow at a specific person, working against them.

So while "inform" = to tell, "inform on" = to tell against someone to a person of authority.
The Grammar — How the Phrase Works

"Inform on" is a phrasal verb (a verb + a preposition that together create a new meaning).

The structure is:

inform on + [the person you are reporting]

Examples of the structure in use:

  • She informed on her neighbour.
  • He refused to inform on his friends.
  • They informed on the gang to the police.

Notice that the person being reported always comes after "on."
The Feeling Behind the Phrase — Its Connotations

This is very important. "Inform on" is not a neutral phrase in feeling, even though it can describe a neutral or even a good act.

In most situations, it carries a negative social feeling — a sense of betrayal, disloyalty, or sneakiness. Society, in many cultures, frowns upon people who "inform on" others, because it feels like going behind someone's back.

Here is the key tension:

  • The person being informed on is usually doing something wrong.
  • But the person doing the informing is often seen as a traitor by the group they belong to.

For example, imagine a group of criminals. If one criminal goes to the police and informs on the others, from the perspective of the law, they did a helpful thing. But from the perspective of the criminal group, they are a traitor — the worst kind.

This is why in everyday informal speech, people use much harsher slang words instead of "inform on" — words like snitch, rat, or grass (British English), because those words carry even more of that feeling of disgust and betrayal.

"Inform on" itself is more formal and neutral in tone compared to those slang words, but the underlying social tension is the same.
When Is Informing on Someone Seen as Positive?

Not always negative. Context matters enormously. For example:

  • A child informs on a classmate who is being bullied by other students → seen as brave and right.
  • A citizen informs on a neighbour who is making explosive devices → seen as responsible and heroic.
  • An employee informs on a manager who is committing financial fraud → seen as courageous (this is often called whistleblowing).

So the act of informing on someone can be morally good or bad depending on who is being reported, why, and to whom.
Synonyms — Other Ways to Say the Same Thing

These all share the same core meaning, but vary in formality and emotional intensity:

Word/PhraseLevel of FormalityNotes
Inform onFormal / NeutralStandard written or spoken English
Tell onInformalUsed mostly by or about children ("He told on me!")
Snitch onVery Informal / SlangStrong feeling of betrayal; very negative tone
Rat onInformal / SlangNegative; the word "rat" compares the person to a dirty animal
Grass onBritish SlangCommon in British English; very negative
BetrayFormalBroader meaning — not just to authorities, but to anyone
ReportFormal / NeutralProfessional contexts; the least negative of all
Tip offInformalTo give a secret warning or piece of information to authorities

Here are examples across different contexts so you can see the phrase in action:

Criminal context:

The suspect agreed to inform on his accomplices in exchange for a lighter sentence.

School context:

Nobody wanted to inform on the students who cheated, because they feared being called a snitch.

War/espionage context:

During the war, some citizens were paid to inform on their neighbours who were hiding enemy soldiers.

Workplace context:

She felt deeply conflicted before deciding to inform on her colleague who had been stealing from the company.

Everyday life:

Even though he saw his brother break the vase, he refused to inform on him to their parents.
A Person Who Does This — The Noun Form

The person who informs on others has specific names:

  • Informer — the most common formal noun.
  • Informant — often used in a police or legal context (e.g., "a police informant").
  • Whistleblower — specifically used when someone reports wrongdoing within an organisation (a company, a government), often with the implication that they are doing the right thing.
  • Snitch / Rat / Grass — slang, all negative.
How It Is Different from Just "Inform"

This is a subtle but crucial distinction:

  • "I informed the police." → You simply told the police something. The sentence doesn't tell us whether you were reporting on a person or just sharing general information.
  • "I informed on my neighbour." → You specifically told the police (or another authority) about your neighbour's wrongdoing. The target is clear.

The preposition "on" is what makes it personal and pointed.
Summary — The Whole Idea in a Few Lines

To inform on someone means to secretly go to a person or group in authority and tell them about something bad that another person has done, with the result that the person gets into trouble. It is a formal phrase, but it carries the feeling of betrayal and disloyalty in most everyday situations. The act itself can be morally right or wrong depending on the situation — but socially, it is almost always seen as a form of going behind someone's back.
